citation.title: A Detailed Anatomical Description of the Gastrocnemius Muscle—Is It Anatomically Positioned to Function as an Antagonist to the Anterior Cruciate Ligament?

accessMethod: Publisher-hosted open full-text HTML opened in the in-app browser; named sections were read, not only a search index or snippet.
editionStatus: Journal publication metadata as shown on the publisher page; article history shows publication on 16 October 2024.

locators.observed: The Achilles tendon was transected and the heads reflected for a 360-degree view; the same procedure was used to calculate the lateral-head femoral attachment.

locators.locator: §4.4, Femoral Attachment of Medial Head of Gastrocnemius, paragraph describing the lateral head
locators.observed: Lateral head described as attaching to the posterior-superior surface of the lateral femoral condyle, proximal to the popliteal muscle tendo.
Authors state they did not directly measure length or width of each condyle and therefore could not calculate the exact percentage occupied by gastrocnemius attachment.

studyDesignAndSample: Cadaveric dissection study; Results §3 reports 22 lower limbs (11 left, 11 right) from 11 embalmed cadavers.
independentAnatomySupport: Independently supports a broad named posterior-superior lateral femoral condyle location for the lateral gastrocnemius head. It supplies no reproducible BodyParts3D triangle list, mesh landmarks, or exact lateral-head footprint boundary transferable to the HUMAN ATLAS femur asset.

searchIndexVsOpenedSource.searchIndex: Discovery aid only; not used as final support.
searchIndexVsOpenedSource.openedSource: Publisher full-text page opened and §§2.2, 4.4, 4.5 read in-browser.
searchIndexVsOpenedSource.humanAnatomyReview: Not performed by a credentialed human reviewer for this project; source inspection is not anatomical approval.

geometryHoldReason: The modern source supplies a broad named region but the mesh review does not expose or map the femoral attachment margin to reproducible triangles or coordinates; its condyle-measurement limitation further precludes deriving a bounded patch. Do not mark the entire bone or estimate vertices/triangles.
